Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Keep the supplied language.", "input": "we had the intercom repair meeting in the laundry room at alder court on tuesday morning because the lobby panel had been cutting out and residents were missing deliveries. i was there with mara ellis from the building office, joel pike from northline access, and mrs chen from 4c, who keeps the paper log for the east entrance. the panel still lit up when we arrived, but the sound dropped whenever somebody pressed the silver call button. joel said the wiring cabinet was dry and the problem seemed to be near the speaker grille, not in the basement power supply. nobody said the unit was ready, and we did not set a date for closing the repair ticket.

mara had printed the service notes from the last two visits and put them beside the sign in sheet. one note said the sound had returned for about an hour after the door closer was adjusted in april. the other said a delivery driver had heard a buzz from the panel but no voice from 4c. mrs chen said she had been home both times and had answered through her kitchen handset. she told us the lobby unit was quieter than that handset, but it was not completely silent. joel asked us not to press the call button over and over because a loose contact could make the test confusing.

we talked first about forwarding the lobby calls to mara's office phone while joel checked the speaker and the cable behind the panel. mara said, “i can keep the office phone near me until four, but i have a lease appointment at half past two.” joel said the forwarding setting could be temporary and would not change the numbers stored for individual apartments. mrs chen asked whether the resident handsets would still ring as usual. joel said they should, and that the test was meant to cover only the lobby call button. he had not tried the temporary setting yet, so nobody treated that as a result.

the office phone sits on a shelf behind the mailboxes, and the signal there is usually steady unless the loading door is open. mara said that on tuesdays the parcel carrier often leaves the loading door propped for a few minutes, even though the sign asks drivers to close it. joel wanted to know whether the phone had to stay at the desk or could be carried to the entrance. mara said it could be carried, but the charging cord was short and the battery indicator had been blinking since monday. we agreed to keep the phone at the desk for the first part of the check and to note the time of each lobby call.

then we went through the work in order. number one inspect the grille for lint and paint, without taking the faceplate off. number two check the small connector behind the panel and make sure the cable was not pinched against the frame. number three use the office phone for forwarding during a single test call, while one person stood in the lobby and another stayed by the desk. number four write down whether the sound was clear at both ends, and whether the door closer or the loading door changed anything. number five return the setting to normal after the test, unless mara asked joel to leave it in place until she had checked with the building manager. joel said he would bring a narrow screwdriver, a flashlight, and two spare clips, but he did not expect to replace the panel.

mrs chen said she could listen from 4c if the test took place before her afternoon medication delivery. she was not asking for the call to be forwarded to her apartment; she wanted to hear whether her own handset sounded different from the lobby speaker. mara wrote that distinction in the margin so nobody would mistake it for a request to change her apartment settings. joel said we could ask her to pick up once, after the lobby test, if she was still home. the delivery usually came between one and two, but the driver had arrived close to noon the previous week, so we left the time flexible.

we also checked what residents had been told. a small notice by the mailboxes said the entrance intercom might be tested, but it did not name a time or say calls could reach the office. mara said she had not sent a building wide message because we did not yet know how long the check would take. mrs chen said some residents do not read the paper notices, especially the people who use the west entrance. joel suggested putting a second notice near that door, and mara said she could do that after the office phone was free. no one asked residents to leave their doors unlocked, and we did not plan to interrupt calls from apartment handsets.

there was one condition that could affect the afternoon plan. if the lobby door was still locked at six because the evening cleaner had not arrived, mara said she would not leave the office phone unattended by the entrance. she could keep it at the desk and ask the caretaker, devon, to stand by the panel for any later test. devon usually arrived at six fifteen, but mara had not confirmed his route for that day. joel said the temporary forwarding could be turned off before he left, and that we should not assume a missed call meant the speaker was fixed or broken. we wrote the condition beside the time notes rather than treating it as a confirmed arrangement.

before we left the laundry room, mara read back the notes aloud and asked whether anything important was missing. mrs chen said to include the faint clicking sound she heard after pressing the call button, and joel added that the click might come from the button itself rather than the speaker. i said the office phone battery and the loading door should both be mentioned, since either could affect what we heard during the test. mara said, “i will keep the phone on the desk, and i will tell you if i have to leave for my appointment.” the final line on the sheet said the next check would depend on joel's arrival time and the office schedule. the repair ticket was still open, and we had not recorded a result from the forwarding test.", "output": "We had the intercom repair meeting in the laundry room at Alder Court on Tuesday morning because the lobby panel had been cutting out and residents were missing deliveries. I was there with Mara Ellis from the building office, Joel Pike from Northline Access, and Mrs. Chen from 4C, who keeps the paper log for the east entrance. The panel still lit up when we arrived, but the sound dropped whenever somebody pressed the silver call button. Joel said the wiring cabinet was dry and the problem seemed to be near the speaker grille, not in the basement power supply. Nobody said the unit was ready, and we did not set a date for closing the repair ticket.

Mara had printed the service notes from the last two visits and put them beside the sign-in sheet. One note said the sound had returned for about an hour after the door closer was adjusted in April. The other said a delivery driver had heard a buzz from the panel but no voice from 4C. Mrs. Chen said she had been home both times and had answered through her kitchen handset. She told us the lobby unit was quieter than that handset, but it was not completely silent. Joel asked us not to press the call button over and over because a loose contact could make the test confusing.

We talked first about forwarding the lobby calls to Mara's office phone while Joel checked the speaker and the cable behind the panel. Mara said, “I can keep the office phone near me until four, but I have a lease appointment at half past two.” Joel said the forwarding setting could be temporary and would not change the numbers stored for individual apartments. Mrs. Chen asked whether the resident handsets would still ring as usual. Joel said they should, and that the test was meant to cover only the lobby call button. He had not tried the temporary setting yet, so nobody treated that as a result.

The office phone sits on a shelf behind the mailboxes, and the signal there is usually steady unless the loading door is open. Mara said that on Tuesdays the parcel carrier often leaves the loading door propped for a few minutes, even though the sign asks drivers to close it. Joel wanted to know whether the phone had to stay at the desk or could be carried to the entrance. Mara said it could be carried, but the charging cord was short and the battery indicator had been blinking since Monday. We agreed to keep the phone at the desk for the first part of the check and to note the time of each lobby call.

Then we went through the work in order. Number one: inspect the grille for lint and paint, without taking the faceplate off. Number two: check the small connector behind the panel and make sure the cable was not pinched against the frame. Number three: use the office phone for forwarding during a single test call, while one person stood in the lobby and another stayed by the desk. Number four: write down whether the sound was clear at both ends, and whether the door closer or the loading door changed anything. Number five: return the setting to normal after the test, unless Mara asked Joel to leave it in place until she had checked with the building manager. Joel said he would bring a narrow screwdriver, a flashlight, and two spare clips, but he did not expect to replace the panel.

Mrs. Chen said she could listen from 4C if the test took place before her afternoon medication delivery. She was not asking for the call to be forwarded to her apartment; she wanted to hear whether her own handset sounded different from the lobby speaker. Mara wrote that distinction in the margin so nobody would mistake it for a request to change her apartment settings. Joel said we could ask her to pick up once, after the lobby test, if she was still home. The delivery usually came between one and two, but the driver had arrived close to noon the previous week, so we left the time flexible.

We also checked what residents had been told. A small notice by the mailboxes said the entrance intercom might be tested, but it did not name a time or say calls could reach the office. Mara said she had not sent a building-wide message because we did not yet know how long the check would take. Mrs. Chen said some residents do not read the paper notices, especially the people who use the west entrance. Joel suggested putting a second notice near that door, and Mara said she could do that after the office phone was free. No one asked residents to leave their doors unlocked, and we did not plan to interrupt calls from apartment handsets.

There was one condition that could affect the afternoon plan. If the lobby door was still locked at six because the evening cleaner had not arrived, Mara said she would not leave the office phone unattended by the entrance. She could keep it at the desk and ask the caretaker, Devon, to stand by the panel for any later test. Devon usually arrived at six fifteen, but Mara had not confirmed his route for that day. Joel said the temporary forwarding could be turned off before he left, and that we should not assume a missed call meant the speaker was fixed or broken. We wrote the condition beside the time notes rather than treating it as a confirmed arrangement.

Before we left the laundry room, Mara read back the notes aloud and asked whether anything important was missing. Mrs. Chen said to include the faint clicking sound she heard after pressing the call button, and Joel added that the click might come from the button itself rather than the speaker. I said the office phone battery and the loading door should both be mentioned, since either could affect what we heard during the test. Mara said, “I will keep the phone on the desk, and I will tell you if I have to leave for my appointment.” The final line on the sheet said the next check would depend on Joel's arrival time and the office schedule. The repair ticket was still open, and we had not recorded a result from the forwarding test."}]
